Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

before six on Thursday, and the kitchen was already warm from the stock pots. The weather had turned wet overnight, so the floor mats near the back door were damp, and the delivery driver had left two crates under the awning rather than bring them inside. Mara was checking the volunteer sheet at the folding table, and she asked me to count the blue aprons before the first group arrived. There were eleven clean aprons and four with loose ties, so we put the clean ones on the right side of the table and tied the loose ones with spare cotton tape. The hall clock was seven minutes fast, but we used it anyway because the wall clock above the sink had stopped again.

The main thing I handled was forwarding the updated pickup note to Devon, the evening coordinator. The note listed the new time for the bread collection and said the bakery van might arrive between seven ten and seven thirty. I checked the paper copy against the message Mara had received and read both times aloud before I forwarded it. I did not change the wording because the bakery had asked us to share the range exactly. Devon was carrying boxes by the pantry door when I told him the note had gone through, and he said, “Good, please leave the range in there. People need to know it is not a promise.” I wrote his comment on the margin of my shift card instead of on the note because the card also had the freezer count and the phone number for the driver.

At the serving counter, we set out cups, spoons, napkins, and a small bowl of wrapped crackers for people waiting before the soup line. The soup that day was lentil with carrots, celery, and lemon, and the second pot held a mild potato stew for anyone who could not have lentils. Jo kept a handwritten ingredient card beside each pot and asked me not to move them when the steam made the card curl. We clipped each card to a clean tray so it stayed readable while the ladles were in use. Two volunteers carried the first trays from the kitchen, and one stayed by the door to check names against the paper list. Nobody had to show identification, and Mara reminded us that a name could be added by phone until half past seven. The visitor book was under the counter beside the spare pencils, and the large-print menu sat at the end where people could reach it.

The three checks before opening were:
1. The hand sink needed soap and paper towels.
2. The allergy cards needed to match the pots.
3. The side aisle had to stay clear for the walker and wheelchair traffic.

I filled the soap dispenser from the sealed bottle and found one roll of towels in the lower cupboard, so I put the last spare roll on the shelf above it. Jo checked the allergy cards against the recipe sheet and called out that the potato stew contained butter while the lentil soup did not. She repeated the information to me, and I placed the cards where nobody would have to lean over the hot pots to read them. The side aisle was clear except for a folded table that had been left near the coat rack. We moved it against the far wall and left the blue tape line visible across the floor so the delivery carts would not be parked there.

If the east entrance is locked after seven, we are supposed to keep the ramp clear and direct late arrivals to the front bell. That instruction mattered later because the east entrance was locked when the next group came through the rain. Devon stayed near the front bell while I held the door, and Mara took the names from the list. One woman said, “My neighbor told me the side door would be open,” and Mara answered, “We have to keep that door locked during service, but the front bell is working.” Nobody was turned away in that exchange, and I heard the bell ring twice while the group came in. We moved the wet floor sign a little farther from the ramp and wiped the water beside the mat without covering the blue tape line.

The bread van had not arrived by seven twenty, so Devon looked at the forwarded note again and called the number written on my shift card. The driver said he was still on the route and expected to reach us before seven thirty. I repeated that estimate to the people waiting near the counter and said it was an estimate rather than a confirmed arrival. One volunteer had started counting the wrapped rolls in the pantry and reported twenty six, but two cartons were still unopened. We left them sealed until the driver got there because the shelf labels for those cartons faced the wall and did not show whether they were seeded or plain. Mara asked me to put a clean cloth over the empty basket and keep it beside the bread table so we could sort the loaves when they arrived. The soup line continued while we waited, and Jo brought a pitcher of water to the end of the counter.

Near the end of the shift, I checked the volunteer sheet again and found that the person assigned to wash the large stock pot had gone home early with a headache. Mara asked whether I could stay ten minutes and rinse it before the next team came in. I said yes after I put the remaining crackers into the sealed container and wrote the count on the pantry card. The delivery tray was still by the door, and the wet coats were hanging on the rack under the window. Devon said the last arrivals had heard about the bread from the note and asked whether the pickup time would be the same next week. I told him the message only covered Thursday and that nobody had confirmed next week's schedule. He wrote a question mark beside the date on his calendar and asked me to leave the driver number on the shift card. I rinsed the pot with warm water while Jo held the handle steady, and the wall clock above the sink stayed stopped when we turned off the kitchen lights."}]
